title: Strive to Enter by the Narrow Door
theme: Responding to news of tragedy, Jesus warns that all must repent or perish, and tells of a fruitless fig tree given one more year. He frees a woman bent over for eighteen years on the Sabbath, teaches that the kingdom grows from small beginnings, and urges people to strive to enter by the narrow door before it is shut. He ends by lamenting over Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and would not be gathered under his wings.

language.note: Twice Jesus says, 'except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.' Instead of speculating about why disasters strike others, every listener must face his own need to turn to God.

Jesus points out that the synagogue ruler would 'loose' his ox on the Sabbath to water it. Ought not this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound, be 'loosed' from her bond on the Sabbath? The Sabbath is a day of liberation.

The root of 'agonize,' used of athletes straining in competition. Entering the kingdom is not a matter of casual interest or mere association with Jesus (v26); it calls for wholehearted response while the door is open.

The 'strait' (narrow) door will one day be shut by the master of the house. Those outside will knock and claim familiarity, but he will say, 'I know you not.' There is a time when the opportunity ends.
Jesus pictures himself as a mother hen longing to gather her chicks under her wings. Scripture often speaks of refuge under God's wings (Psalm 91:4), and Jesus applies that divine image to himself.

usage.note: Job's friends assumed suffering proved special guilt. Jesus rejects that conclusion while insisting that all are sinners who need to repent.

usage.theme: Israel as God's vine and fig tree
usage.note: God looked for fruit from his people and found none. The fig tree parable warns Israel of judgment while showing God's patience.
The prophets foresaw peoples coming from every direction to feast with God. Jesus says they will sit down in the kingdom while some who expected to be there are cast out.
God shelters his people under his wings. Jerusalem refused that shelter.

context.setting: Chapter 13 continues the journey to Jerusalem, now with an urgent call to repentance. The incidents Jesus mentions, Galileans killed by Pilate while sacrificing and eighteen killed by a falling tower in Siloam, are not recorded elsewhere, but fit what is known of Pilate's violence and Jerusalem's building works. Verse 22 reminds the reader that Jesus is 'journeying toward Jerusalem,' and the chapter closes with his lament over the city that will reject him.

flow.label: Repent or perish
flow.note: Jesus says the Galileans killed by Pilate and those crushed by the tower of Siloam were not worse sinners than others; unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.

flow.label: The barren fig tree
flow.note: A fig tree without fruit for three years is given one more year of care before it is cut down.

flow.label: A daughter of Abraham freed
flow.note: On the Sabbath Jesus heals a woman bent over for eighteen years; the synagogue ruler objects, and Jesus shames his opponents while the people rejoice.

flow.label: Mustard seed and leaven
flow.note: The kingdom is like a mustard seed that becomes a tree and leaven that spreads through all the dough.

flow.label: The narrow door
flow.note: Asked if few will be saved, Jesus says strive to enter the narrow door; many will be shut out while people come from east and west to the feast; the last will be first.

flow.label: Lament over Jerusalem
flow.note: Warned that Herod wants to kill him, Jesus calls him 'that fox,' says a prophet cannot perish outside Jerusalem, and mourns over the city that would not be gathered.

tier1.note: 'Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the LORD.' Jesus quotes the psalm, which the crowds will sing at his entry (19:38).
'Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity.'

tier2.note: God's vineyard yielded wild grapes, and he announced judgment on it.
'This house shall become a desolation.' Jesus warns that Jerusalem's house will be left desolate.
The narrow gate and the warning to those who claim association with Jesus but are not known by him.
Birds nesting in the branches of a great tree, an image of a kingdom sheltering the nations.

tier3.note: God plants a tender twig that becomes a cedar where birds of every kind dwell.
Matthew's version of the lament over Jerusalem.
The Lord is patient, not wishing that any should perish, as the vinedresser asks for one more year.

voices.name: Joel B. Green
voices.work: The Gospel of Luke (New International Commentary on the New Testament)
voices.view: Green emphasizes that Jesus calls the woman a 'daughter of Abraham' (v16), restoring her to full status in God's people. He sees the healing as a picture of the release Jesus announced at Nazareth, enacted on the Sabbath, the day meant to celebrate God's deliverance.

voices.name: J. C. Ryle
voices.work: Expository Thoughts on the Gospels: Luke
voices.view: Ryle drew from the question 'are there few that be saved?' the lesson that Jesus turns curiosity about others into a personal call. Rather than speculate about how many will be saved, each person should strive to be among them.

translations.kjv: Strive to enter in at the strait gate: for many, I say unto you, will seek to enter in, and shall not be able.

renderings.text: Strive to enter through the narrow door
Make every effort to enter through the narrow door

translations.note: 'Strait' means narrow, not 'straight.' Older manuscripts read 'door' (thyra) rather than 'gate' (pylē), matching the house and closed door of verse 25. Matthew 7:13 speaks of a narrow gate.

translations.kjv: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent unto thee; how often would I have gathered thy children together, as a hen doth gather her brood under her wings, and ye would not!

renderings.text: as a hen gathers her brood under her wings
as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings

translations.note: The versions agree closely. 'How often' suggests Jesus had sought to gather Jerusalem more than once, which fits John's account of several visits to the city.

steps.gospel: The chapter holds together judgment and patience. All need to repent (v3, 5), but God, like the vinedresser, gives time and care before judgment (v8-9). Jesus sets free a daughter of Abraham whom Satan had bound (v16), showing what his kingdom does. The door into the kingdom is narrow, Jesus himself, and it will not stay open forever, but it is open to people from east, west, north and south (v29). Jesus' longing to gather Jerusalem like a hen shows the heart of God, and he will go on to that city to die for those who reject him.
application: When tragedy strikes, examine your own heart rather than judging the victims.
Do not presume on God's patience. The extra year is a mercy meant to lead to fruit.
Value people the way Jesus does, restoring dignity to those others overlook.
Take the narrow door seriously. Familiarity with Jesus is not the same as knowing him.
Share Jesus' grief over those who refuse his care, and pray for them.

misapplications.claim: Victims of disasters must have committed especially terrible sins.
misapplications.correction: Jesus says plainly, 'I tell you, Nay' (v3, 5). The disasters are warnings to everyone to repent, not proof of special guilt.

misapplications.claim: Since God is patient, there is no urgency about repentance.
misapplications.correction: The fig tree has one more year (v9) and the door will be shut (v25). Patience is an opportunity, not an indefinite delay.

misapplications.claim: Having eaten and drunk in Jesus' presence or heard his teaching is enough.
misapplications.correction: Those who say 'we have eaten and drunk in thy presence' are told 'I know you not' (v26-27). Knowing about Jesus is not the same as entering through him.

contrasts.note: If animals are cared for on the Sabbath, how much more a suffering woman.
The kingdom's beginnings are small, its end vast.

features.label: Two current events
features.note: Jesus draws on two recent news stories, one a human atrocity and one an accident, to teach the same lesson (v1-5).

features.label: Eighteen and eighteen
features.note: Eighteen died at Siloam (v4) and the woman had been bound eighteen years (v11, 16), perhaps linking the two scenes of death and release.

features.label: Twin parables
features.note: A man's mustard seed and a woman's leaven (v18-21) give paired illustrations, a pattern Luke uses often (15:3-10).

features.label: 'That fox'
features.note: Jesus calls Herod a fox, a symbol of craftiness or insignificance, and refuses to be deflected from his appointed path (v32-33).

steps.summary: Luke 13 issues an urgent call to repentance: disasters are warnings to all, God's patience has limits, and the narrow door will be shut. Yet Jesus also shows the liberating power of the kingdom, freeing a bent woman on the Sabbath and promising that the kingdom will grow to embrace people from every direction. The chapter closes with his sorrowful lament over Jerusalem, which refuses his shelter.

metaArc.book: Chapter 13 continues the journey with rising urgency, and its lament over Jerusalem (v34-35) points to Jesus' arrival and weeping over the city in chapter 19.
metaArc.redemptive: The chapter shows Redemption as release from Satan's bondage and an invitation to all nations, while warning of judgment on those who refuse it.
